title: Modeling heading and path perception from optic flow in the case of independently moving objects
abstract: Humans are usually accurate when estimating heading or path from optic flow, even in the presence of independently moving objects (IMOs) in an otherwise rigid scene. To invoke significant biases in perceived heading, IMOs have to be large and obscure the focus of expansion (FOE) in the image plane, which is the point of approach. For the estimation of path during curvilinear self-motion no significant biases were found in the presence of IMOs. We derive analytical models of optic flow for linear and curvilinear self-motion using geometric scene models. Heading biases of a linear least squares method, which builds upon these analytical models, are large, larger than those reported for humans. This motivated us to study segmentation cues that are available from optic flow. We derive models of accretion/deletion, expansion/contraction, acceleration/deceleration, local spatial curvature, and local temporal curvature, to be used as cues to segment an IMO from the background. Integrating these segmentation cues into our method of estimating heading or path now explains human psychophysical data and extends, as well as unifies, previous investigations. Our analysis suggests that various cues available from optic flow help to segment IMOs and, thus, make humans' heading and path perception robust in the presence of such IMOs.
introduction: Humans are robust in estimating heading/path from optic flow even with independently moving objects (IMOs), with significant biases only occurring if IMOs are large and obscure the focus of expansion (FOE) for heading, but no significant biases for curvilinear path perception. This study aims to understand the mechanisms enabling this robustness by deriving analytical models of optic flow and flow-based segmentation cues.
methods: Analytical models for optic flow were derived for linear and curvilinear self-motion in various scene configurations (plane, ground plane). Linear least squares methods were developed to estimate heading (FOE) and path (radius). Five segmentation cues were modeled: accretion/deletion, expansion/contraction, acceleration/deceleration, local spatial curvature, and local temporal curvature. These cues were integrated into the estimation methods by weighting flow from IMO regions. Models were evaluated against psychophysical data from Warren and Saunders (1995), Royden and Hildreth (1996), and Fajen and Kim (2002).
results: Without segmentation cues, the model showed larger heading biases than humans, especially for non-crossing and crossing IMO paths. Integrating segmentation cues significantly improved the model's fit to human psychophysical data, explaining the robustness of heading and path perception in the presence of IMOs. Segmentation cues like accretion/deletion, expansion/contraction, and acceleration/deceleration showed strong differences (>30%) between static and dynamic discontinuities in most evaluated cases, indicating their utility for IMO segmentation.
discussion: The study suggests that various optic flow-based segmentation cues (accretion/deletion, expansion/contraction, acceleration/deceleration, spatial/temporal curvature) are crucial for humans' robust heading and path perception in the presence of IMOs. These cues help reduce or discard the IMO's influence on motion integration, explaining seemingly contradictory results across different psychophysical studies based on the specific cues available in each experimental condition. The analytical models provide a mechanistic explanation for initial segmentation, complementing existing flow parsing, motion-opponent, and iterative estimation models.

limitations: Temporal integration was excluded for simplicity, assuming an instantaneous flow field.
Eye movements, head movements, and body movements were not included in the model equations.
Higher order temporal changes (e.g., accelerations in 3D motion) were excluded from the motion model.
Local spatial and temporal curvature cues were excluded from the combined segmentation cue due to analytical difficulties in finding corresponding line integrals.
